summary: Describes how the IP multicast service being developed for ATM networks can be used to support IP broadcast. Since ATM has no native broadcast, one is built from multicast.

plainLanguage.summary: ATM networks cannot shout to everyone at once. This shows how to fake it by sending to a group that includes everyone.

questions: how to do ip broadcast over atm
how does ip broadcast work over atm
why does bootp need the all ones broadcast
what is the atm broadcast channel
subtitle: How to fake IP broadcast on ATM, a network with no broadcast, by treating it as a multicast group of everyone.

tldr.problem: ATM is built from point-to-point and point-to-multipoint connections and has no native broadcast, yet some IP applications such as bootp clients and RIP depend on broadcast.
tldr.mechanism: Every host in a Logical IP Subnet joins the 255.255.255.255 group at the MARS. Broadcasts are then sent on a point-to-multipoint VC to that group's members, the broadcast channel.
tldr.outcome: No change to the MARS is needed, since broadcast is just one more multicast group. It is a Proposed Standard that builds on RFC 2022.

today: RFC 2226 is a Proposed Standard published in October 1997, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the MARS architecture of RFC 2022.

sections.title: The Missing Broadcast
sections.content:
RFC 1577 handled unicast over ATM inside Logical IP Subnets (LISs) with a central ATM ARP Server. It left out multicast and broadcast. RFC 2022 added multicast through the MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server), which keeps mappings between IP multicast addresses and groups of ATM addresses.

This memo shows how RFC 2022 can emulate IP broadcast within a LIS. The authors admit that broadcast fits ATM poorly, but some applications still need it. A client searching for a server by broadcast is one case, and routing protocols such as RIP are another.
sections.plainLanguage: ATM is like a phone network where you can only call people one by one. This RFC finds a way to still make an announcement to everyone.

sections.title: Unicast and Multicast on ATM
sections.content:
A unicast IP address has one ATM destination, reached over a point-to-point Virtual Channel (VC). A host asks the ARP Server with an ARP_REQUEST and gets an ARP_REPLY or an ARP_NAK.

Multicast works similarly, but the sender must build and manage a point-to-multipoint VC whose leaves are the group members. Under UNI 3.1 only the source (root) can create or change such a VC.

The MARS keeps each group's member list. Hosts register with MARS_JOIN and withdraw with MARS_LEAVE, and these messages are passed on to group members so senders can adjust their VCs. To send to a Class D address, a host sends a MARS_REQUEST and gets back a MARS_MULTI carrying ATM addresses, or a MARS_NAK if there is no mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper keeps a list of who belongs to each group. Before talking to a group, you ask the helper for the list, then call everyone on it.

sections.title: Broadcast as a Special Multicast Group
sections.content:
The key idea is that broadcast is a multicast group whose members are everyone in the LIS. Two broadcast addresses are covered: the 255.255.255.255 "all ones" limited broadcast, and the CIDR-prefix (subnet) directed broadcast, where the host part is all ones. At the link layer both reach the same place: every member of the LIS gets a copy.

On Ethernet both end up at the same stations. On ATM there is no broadcast medium, so stations must register, and if they registered for some groups and not others the groups would have different memberships and broadcast would become inconsistent.

Diskless boot settles the choice. A bootp client does not know its own IP address or subnet mask, so it can only use the all ones group. The bootp server must reply on that same group. Therefore the all ones group in MARS MUST be used by all LIS members when registering to receive broadcast. The VCC used to send any broadcast packet is called the broadcast channel.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone joins one big "everybody" group. A newcomer who does not yet know where they live can still reach everyone through it.

sections.title: What the MARS Does and Does Not Change
sections.content:
The RFC keeps some features of the MARS architecture as they are:

  • The MARS has no knowledge of subnet prefixes or masks, and manages each group address independently.
  • A MARS may serve only one LIS, so the all ones group is joined by hosts from one LIS and keeps its usual scope.
  • A Multicast Server (MCS) from RFC 2022 may serve the broadcast group without modification, which reduces the number of channels.

The MARS needs no new code to resolve broadcast addresses. It is a general database of {protocol address, ATM.1, ... ATM.n} mappings, and whether hosts see an address as Class D or broadcast is purely a host matter. Because boot-time hosts may not know their IP address, the MARS should NOT expect both the IP source and ATM source fields of MARS_JOIN to be filled in.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper just keeps lists and does not care what a list is for, so a list called "everybody" needs no special treatment.

sections.title: Host Requirements
sections.content:
A host that supports broadcast this way must:

  • register as a MARS client;
  • soon after registering, issue a MARS_JOIN to 255.255.255.255 with mar$flags.layer3grp reset;
  • map all IP-layer broadcasts it sends to the broadcast channel built from the all ones entry;
  • monitor MARS_JOIN and MARS_LEAVE for 255.255.255.255 to keep that channel current.

A broadcast channel should be torn down after inactivity. The timeout MAY be set with a minimum of one minute, and the RECOMMENDED default is 20 minutes.

Every participant MUST be in the all ones group, but not all will transmit, so a LIS of n stations may have fewer than n channels ending at each station. An MCS could cut that to two VCs (one in, one out), or one for a listen-only station. Because broadcast can tax network and host resources, an implementer MAY offer a way to withdraw from the group with MARS_LEAVE, but the default SHALL be to join.
sections.plainLanguage: Each computer must sign up for the everybody group when it arrives, and hang up the line if nobody has used it for a while.

sections.title: Cost and Open Questions
sections.content:
By default, multicast uses meshes of point-to-multipoint VCs straight from source to members. The broadcast group will be the biggest consumer of VCs in the ATM network when active, so it will likely be the first group given an MCS. Administrators can do this transparently to hosts, group by group.

The RFC leaves some issues open. The ATM address of the MARS must be configured by hand into a diskless workstation, and ideas such as universal channel numbers or universal ATM addresses found no agreement. MARS is protocol independent, so similar addresses could be found for other layer 3 protocols. Some people also wanted a link-layer broadcast independent of layer 3.
sections.plainLanguage: Because everyone must hear the announcement, it uses a lot of phone lines. A switchboard in the middle can save lines.

sections.title: Security and Rejected Alternatives
sections.content:
The security implications are no greater or less than those of using any other multicast group. Any added security would have to be an extension to the RFC 2022 architecture.

Appendix A records alternatives that were dropped. Using the unmodified RFC 1577 ARP Server, a host would send an ARP request for every LIS member, which loads the server heavily, does not scale, cannot transparently use an MCS, and fails for diskless boot. An enhanced ARP Server that adds MARS_MULTI still has the VC scaling and diskless boot problems, and fixing the latter would make the ARP Server look more like a MARS.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors tried simpler plans first, but they were too slow or could not help a computer that does not yet know its own address.
